A B S T R A C T
Passenger transit hub is a quintessential complex system, characterized by intricate interac-
tions among humans, facilities, and the surrounding environment. External disturbances often
precipitate crowd congestion and safety risks. Modeling the spatial–temporal distribution of
passenger flow within the hub is an important element in operational management. Prevailing
research predominantly focuses on static models or monitoring data to assess the spatial–
temporal characteristics of passenger flow throughout the hub. Nevertheless, few studies have
been found in modeling passenger flow distribution for passenger transit hub from the vantage
point of traveler behavior in the intricate ‘human-facility-environment’ complex network. Thus,
this paper proposes a computational model for the passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution
based on traveler behavior. First, combining consideration of critical spatial facilities and
passenger flow streamlines, a passenger flow network is established. Second, the instantaneous
travel times of link and node are defined while considering queuing and congestion at crucial
facilities in the hub. Then, a passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model for the
passenger transit hub is constructed, which consists of dynamic route choice model and dynamic
passenger flow loading model. A solution algorithm is simultaneously designed. Finally, the
effectiveness of the model and algorithm are verified by a numerical example. The results
show that the proposed model can effectively capture real-time congestion and the dynamic
distribution of passenger flow in the hub. Therefore, this study contributes to the safety
management and layout optimization of the hub, holding significant importance for improving
hub operational efficiency and service levels.
1. Introduction
Passenger transit hubs stand as indispensable components of the transportation system, representing foundational prerequisites
for its effective operation. When passenger transit hubs face external disturbances, such as a sudden increase in passenger density
during peak hours or a decrease in service capacity due to facility malfunctions, it can easily lead to widespread congestion and
even stampede incidents. Improper handling of risk events in hubs can lead to serious political, economic, and social consequences.
Therefore, modeling the dynamic distribution of passenger flow within hubs can assist operators in adjusting strategies and resource
allocation promptly, thereby enhancing operational efficiency and service levels. Additionally, when facing unforeseen events, it can
effectively address passenger congestion, safety risks, and more, ensuring the safety and smoothness of passenger travel.
Currently, the literature on pedestrian flow research primarily addresses two aspects: the micro-level and macro-level, and
they model pedestrian flow from different perspectives (Duives et al., 2013). In micro-level models, each pedestrian is treated

Conversely, in macro-level models, pedestrians are analyzed as a whole, disregarding specific behaviors of individual pedestrians,
and focusing on the overall movement patterns of pedestrian flow, such as density, flow, speed, etc. These models are suitable for
studying overall trends and large-scale changes (Hoogendoorn et al., 2015; Zanariah et al., 2014).
The micro-level models constitute a crucial component in the field of pedestrian flow research, garnering extensive attention
and application over the past few decades. One type of micro-level model is the cellular automaton model, which discretizes
space into cells and governs pedestrian movement decisions based on specific rules and the states of neighboring cells, thereby
simulating the overall dynamics of pedestrian flow (Blue and Adler, 1998; Zhou et al., 2023). However, the computation speed
of this model is significantly influenced by the size of the population. Helbing and Molnar (1995) introduced the second type of
micro-level model, known as the social force model. This model, grounded in principles of physics, conceptualizes interactions
between pedestrians as a series of forces, aiming to simulate pedestrian movement and interactions in diverse environments (Chen
et al., 2018). Subsequently, with the advancement of computer technology and the development of complex systems theory, agent-
based models have been employed in pedestrian flow research. These models can more accurately simulate individual behaviors
and decision-making processes, making them suitable for complex scenarios (Berceanu et al., 2022; Hassanpour and Rassafi, 2021;
Kim and Kim, 2023). Additionally, some studies utilize crowd dynamics to consider interactions between individuals and collective
behaviors, aiming to simulate and analyze macroscopic characteristics of large-scale crowds (Bruno et al., 2011; Jiang and Zhang,
2012). A comparison of different models in pedestrian flow research, along with their advantages and shortcomings, is detailed
in Table 1. In general, micro-level models are more detailed and suitable for research scenarios focusing on individual behaviors
and local interactions. Considering that such models typically require detailed computation and simulation of each pedestrian’s
characteristics, destination, and interactive behaviors, the computational workload required in any large-scale infrastructure is
usually substantial. (Duives et al., 2013).
Common macroscopic pedestrian flow models mainly include statistical models, continuum models, and network-based models.
For detailed descriptions and comparisons of these models, please refer to Table 1 (Duives et al., 2013). Statistical models use
statistical and mathematical methods to model and analyze real pedestrian flow data, uncovering patterns and characteristics of
pedestrian flow, such as establishing fundamental diagrams (Daamen et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Continuum
models are mathematical models used to describe the movement of large-scale crowds (Goatin et al., 2009; Hughes, 2000). For
instance, some studies treat crowds as continuous fluids and use fluid dynamics models to describe the flow characteristics of
crowds (Helbing, 1998; Henderson, 1974). Colombo and Rosini (2005) discussed a model based on the classical Lighthill–Whitam
and Richards (LWR) model. Hoogendoorn et al. (2015) proposed a macroscopic multi-class continuum model that considers route
choice behavior on both the strategic (pre-trip) and tactical (en-route) level. Network-based models abstract the spatial environment
into a network structure and utilize network theory to describe and analyze pedestrian movement and interactions in space (Hänseler
et al., 2017; Zheng and Mou, 2023). Unlike micro-level models, macroscopic models are not intended to simulate the behavior of
individual pedestrians. Instead, these models may offer predictions when there is a need to estimate the overall characteristics of
crowd movement, such as speed, density, and flow rate these models may offer useful predictions when there is a need to estimate
the overall characteristics of crowd movement, such as speed, density, and flow rate (Lam and Cheung, 2000; Patra et al., 2017).
Due to the significantly lower computational burden of macroscopic models compared to microscopic ones, particularly in scenarios
where fast simulation with lower accuracy is required, macroscopic models offer a favorable alternative (Hoogendoorn et al., 2015).
Through the analysis above, it can be observed that some existing pedestrian flow models still have certain limitations when
modeling the dynamic passenger flow within transportation hubs. For example, microscopic models focus on individual behaviors
and interactions, making them complex and unsuitable for describing the movement of large crowds. Existing macroscopic models,
such as continuum models, are typically described in the form of partial differential equations or integral equations, making their
establishment and solution highly complex. On the other hand, statistical models based on real data have a strong dependence on
the data and can only describe existing features, lacking predictive capabilities. These characteristics render them unsuitable for
application within hubs.
Due to the large scale and complex internal structure of transportation hubs, pedestrian flows often exhibit intricate structures
and dynamic changes. Therefore, this study employs a macroscopic network-based model to analyze and model them. Such models
offer several advantages: (1) Network-based models can effectively capture the overall characteristics and behavioral patterns of
passenger flows within hubs, enabling managers to grasp the overall trends of passenger flows in real-time. (2) Such models offer
faster simulation speeds and lower computational costs. By adjusting network structures, link and node information, and passenger
flow data, a large number of simulation results can be generated in a short period, catering to various application scenarios. (3)
They can provide more planning and optimization information, such as optimal route planning and facility layout optimization.
This information is highly valuable for planners and managers, assisting them in formulating more rational strategies.
The existing literature constructed passenger flow network in the hub by treating the crucial location as node and passenger
trajectory as link. For example, Zheng and Mou (2023) modeled a hub station as a network, representing facilities and equipment
as nodes, and defined edges based on spatial adjacency. The data for nodes and edges included passenger flow, average velocity,
and other relevant traffic parameters. Yue et al. (2019) divided functional areas based on the spatial layout and activity type
of the passenger transit hub, and constructed a passenger flow network according to passengers’ movement paths. Li and Zhang
(2023) defined nodes as geometric feature points within the service area and defined links as horizontal or vertical pedestrian
passage facilities, employing the L-space method to establish a streamline network of the transportation hub complex. In general,
the internal network construction of a passenger transit hub is often based on its spatial layout or passenger flow streamlines,
and the comprehensive consideration of these two factors is crucial. This is because passenger flow streamlines capture the

understanding and prediction of passenger behaviors. Meanwhile, the spatial layout of the hub reflects the internal spatial structure
and the distribution of various functional facilities, such as platforms, ticket offices and waiting areas, which helps determine the
connectivity, accessibility, and capacity of different functional areas. However, constructing a passenger flow network involves more

densities, and travel times. For example, Ren et al. (2014) established an evacuation path network for a subway station that considers

and corridors, and node impedances at doorways, fare gates, and points of capacity reduction. It should be noted that the travel time

locations where throughput capacity decreases, resulting in delays or queues when passengers pass through, while others do not.
The passenger flow network within transportation hubs is highly complex, consisting of multiple channels, exits, and various
service facilities. Passengers within it typically engage in route choice behavior (Stubenschrott et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2023;
Hoogendoorn and Bovy, 2002). In practice, passengers within hubs aim to reach platforms or exits as quickly as possible, dynamically
choosing the shortest route based on real-time conditions. In existing studies, some scholars have applied static traffic assignment
models to pedestrian flow networks (Lilasathapornkit et al., 2022; Khalid et al., 2020; Aalami and Kattan, 2020). These models
can predict pedestrian route choices and distributions to some extent. In transportation hubs, there are also scholars who use
static traffic assignment models to reflect pedestrian distributions. For example, Hänseler et al. (2016) utilized a traffic assignment
model to describe the propagation of pedestrians through stations, providing estimates of general traffic conditions regarding flow,
walking time, speed, and density. However, such static-based models cannot simulate real-time pedestrian movements and time-
varying distributions within the network. To depict phenomena such as the movement, congestion, aggregation, or dispersion
of passenger flow within a hub, corresponding macroscopic models can be established using the theory of Dynamic Traffic
Assignment (DTA). From the perspective of pedestrian behavior, DTA models are suitable for describing the dynamic distribution
of pedestrians (Gao et al., 2014). Although numerous DTA models have been proposed for road traffic networks (Batista et al.,
2021), literature introducing DTA models to describe pedestrian flow is limited. Aghamohammadi and Laval (2020) conducted a
comprehensive literature review on DTA models for pedestrian flow and vehicle flow. Hänseler et al. (2017) proposed a dynamic

In existing research on network-based pedestrian flow models, some scholars have applied static traffic assignment models to
hubs. While such studies to some extent reflect passengers’ route choice behavior within hubs, they fail to capture the dynamic
characteristics of passenger flow distribution over time. In pedestrian flow research, there are also dynamic network-based models,
such as DTA models. However, the passenger flow network within the hub differs significantly from general pedestrian flow
networks. Various types of infrastructure within the hub typically possess service and functional characteristics, yet existing
models overlook passenger queuing at service facilities and bottleneck areas within the hub. In summary, for special scenarios
like hubs, there has not been research that simultaneously models passengers’ dynamic route choice behavior and the dynamic
distribution of passenger flows using network-based models. Therefore, our model can be considered one of the earliest studies on
the spatial–temporal distribution of passenger flow in a hub scenario.
This study proposes a passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model that considers the queuing at critical nodes, based on
a passenger flow network within the hub. The main contributions of this study are as follows:
(1) A passenger flow network is established based on the actual layout and streamlines within the hub. The congestion at various
types of passage facilities and queuing at service facilities and bottleneck areas is described using travel time models. This approach
aligns more closely with the spatial structure of the hub and its unique functional and service features.
(2) The passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model can dynamically update the distribution of passenger flow within the
hub over time based on the time-varying inflow rate. Moreover, the obtained results are generally consistent with those of mature
simulation platforms, indicating good model performance.
(3) The model established in this paper considers passenger flow as a whole, no longer focusing on individual behaviors.
Compared to other models, it offers faster computation speed and is not influenced by the scale of pedestrians. This makes it more
suitable for densely populated large-scale environments like transportation hubs.
(4) This network-based model possesses the optimal solution, allowing for subsequent optimization of streamlines and facility
layout within the hub based on this model. This expands the model’s application scope and practical significance.
The structure of this paper is as follows. Section 2 establishes a passenger flow network within the hub and the corresponding
travel time model. Section 3 establishes a passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model within the hub and designs solution
algorithms. Section 4 devises a numerical example to validate that the proposed model can describe real-time congestion and
the dynamic distribution of passenger flows within different areas of the hub under different scenarios. Section 5 draws several
conclusions and provides recommendations for future work.
2. Network construction in a passenger transit hub
2.1. Passenger flow network construction
The passenger’s activities within the hub occur in a certain sequence. Due to the different of passenger’s activities, the types of
passenger flow in the hub are also different, which mainly include inbound passenger flow and outbound passenger flow. Inbound
passenger flow refers to passengers arriving at the hub from various traffic modes and entering the hub, forming a flow that proceeds
through a series of activities within the hub before reaching the platforms. On the other hand, outbound passenger flow refers to
passengers leaving the platform and exiting the hub to access various traffic modes. In constructing the passenger flow network
within the hub, this paper only considers passengers’ typical activities within the hub. Non-essential activities such as shopping,
dining, and restroom visits are not taken into account. The typical sequence of events for most inbound passengers is as follows:
arrival, inquiry, ticket purchase, baggage check-in, waiting, ticket checking, and boarding. For outbound passengers, the sequence
includes alighting, exit ticket checking, retrieving baggage, and transferring to other modes of transportation. Different types of
passenger flow within the hub can be represented as streamlines which can be described by a flow chart. When focusing on
passengers’ main activities within the hub, the process diagrams for inbound and outbound passenger flow streamlines are depicted
in Fig. 1.
On a macroscopic level, the passenger flow streamlines reflect the route which passenger take within the hub. Obviously, the flow
streamline is also a collection of passenger movement trajectories. Therefore, this paper establishes a hub passenger flow network
based on passenger flow streamlines. Because inbound and outbound passenger flows operate independently without interference,
the established hub passenger flow network can be further divided into two subnetworks: the inbound passenger flow subnetwork
and the outbound passenger flow subnetwork. The inbound passenger flow subnetwork is constructed based on inbound passenger
flow streamlines, incorporating the layout of inbound facilities and the spatial structure. Similarly, the outbound passenger flow
subnetwork is established by considering outbound passenger flow streamlines, layout of outbound facilities, and spatial structure.

Functional nodes refer to the facilities within the hub that provide services and areas where critical activities occur along
passenger flow streamlines, such as security checks, ticket offices, waiting areas, ticket gates, etc. At these nodes, passengers have
obvious gathering and dispersal behavior, as illustrated in Fig. 3. Passengers gather from various directions at functional nodes
and disperse independently after receiving services. When passenger flow is high, waiting passengers may experience queuing. If
queuing becomes severe, localized congestion can occur in the hub, reducing efficiency for passengers moving through that area.
Therefore, the operational efficiency of functional nodes plays a crucial role in the overall operation of the hub.

2.2. A travel time model
According to the defined passenger flow network, passengers’ travel time within the hub includes two components: the transit
time of links and the delay time at nodes. These can be described by link travel time and node travel time, respectively. Due to
the complex internal structure of passenger transit hubs, high passenger density, and strong mobility, the number of passengers on
each link and node in the hub passenger flow network changes over time. Therefore, the travel time of different links and nodes at
different moments is also variable.
At any given time 𝑘, the actual travel time of a link or node refers to the actual transit time of passengers on that link or the
actual delay time at that node when passengers enter the link or arrive at the node at time 𝑘. Since the distribution of passengers
on links and nodes in the hub network varies over time, the actual transit time or delay time at the moment when passengers enter
a link or arrive at a node is unknown; it is only known once passengers have completed their journey through the link or passed
through the node. In other words, the actual travel time is influenced by the changing passenger flow at any given time. Therefore,
in all constructed models and algorithms, the actual travel time at time 𝑘is not known and can only be estimated.
Therefore, the instantaneous travel time at time 𝑘can be used to approximate the actual travel time. The instantaneous travel
time of any link or node at time 𝑘refers to the time required for passengers to pass through the link or the delay time at the node,
assuming that the passenger flow conditions remain unchanged at that moment (Ran and Boyce, 2012).
In constructing the passenger travel time model within the hub, the following assumptions are made. First, no distinction is made
between passenger types, such as age, gender, or whether they are carrying luggage. Second, the transit time through links and the
delay at nodes are only influenced by the inherent properties of the links and nodes themselves and the current flow conditions.
Third, the travel time between links and nodes is independent of each other, meaning the travel time is not affected by other links
or nodes.
(1) Instantaneous link travel time
The transit time of the link within the hub is primarily influenced by the physical characteristics of the link, the current passenger
density on the link, and the walking speed of passengers. Among these factors, the physical characteristics of the link encompass
parameters such as link type, length, width, height, gradient, and more. The passenger density on the link is related to the number of
passengers and dynamically changes over time. Passenger walking speed is primarily correlated with the current passenger density
on the link. The links in the hub passenger flow network can be divided into two types: stair units with elevation difference and
passageways without elevation difference.
The parameters to describe the physical characteristics of passageway include length and width. It can be assumed that passengers
on the same link within the hub will maintain approximately the same movement speed at a given moment. Therefore, the movement
of passenger flow can be treated as uniform motion in space. In this uniform motion, passenger density largely influences passengers’
walking speed. When the passenger density on a link is high, congestion increases, leading to a lower average walking speed for
passengers. Conversely, when the passenger density on a link is low, congestion decreases, resulting in a higher average walking
speed for passengers.
The relationship between speed and density is the most important characteristic of pedestrian flow, also referred to as the
fundamental diagram. The earliest research on the speed-density relationship was conducted within the field of traffic flow. Table 2

(2) Instantaneous node travel time
In the hub passenger flow network defined in this paper, nodes are mainly categorized into three types: origin–destination nodes,
functional nodes, and virtual nodes. Functional nodes possess strong service and functional characteristics, which can lead to the
aggregation and congestion of passengers. When passengers pass through narrowed areas or links obstructed by obstacles, queues can
easily form due to changes in throughput capacity, creating bottlenecks. Therefore, disregarding travel time at the origin–destination
nodes, the node travel time defined in this paper represents the delay time experienced by pedestrians at functional nodes and virtual
nodes where the throughput capacity is reduced.
Functional nodes in the hub passenger flow network encompass functional areas or service facilities such as security checks, ticket
offices, waiting areas, ticket gates, and so on. At these functional nodes, queuing and waiting phenomena occur when passengers’
arrival rate exceeds the facility’s service rate. Thus, each functional node can be treated as an independent queuing system, where
passengers are served in the order of arrival. According to experience, it is assumed that the arrival rate of passengers within a
certain time interval follows a Poisson distribution. Multiple service facilities are considered to be independent of each other, and
their average service rates are equal (𝜇1 = 𝜇2 = ⋯= 𝜇𝑐= 𝜇). This allows the use of the standard M/M/c queuing model to describe
passengers’ behavior when passing through functional nodes, as depicted in Fig. 6.

3. A passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model
The passenger inflow rates of the hub change over time, giving the network a dynamic nature. Therefore, this paper establishes
a passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model. This model consists of a passenger route choice model based on dynamic
stochastic user equilibrium and a dynamic passenger loading model. The model’s framework is illustrated in Fig. 8.
The passenger movement in the passenger flow network within the hub can be divided into two levels: the route and link levels.
At the route level, the route choice model determines the direction and path of passengers within the hub. At the link level, the
dynamic loading model describes the specific movement of passengers within the hub. Simultaneously, the route choice model,
combined with the dynamic inflow rate of passenger flow, provides the passenger inflow rates on various routes at the current
moment, which serves as input for the dynamic loading model. The dynamic loading model calculates the inflow and outflow rates
and the number of passengers for each link and node at each period. This allows updating the instantaneous travel time at links
and nodes, ultimately influencing the passengers’ route choice behavior for the next period.
The passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model established in this paper is based on the following assumptions: (1)
Passengers do not change their chosen route once they have initially selected it and will proceed along this route until reaching their
destination. (2) Passengers have a complete understanding of the infrastructure within the hub and the resulting route options. (3)
The diversity of passenger behavior is disregarded, assuming that all passengers exhibit similar behavioral patterns, and individual
behavioral differences are not considered to affect passenger flow.

3.1. Dynamic route choice model
Passenger transit hubs generally have complex internal structures and numerous passenger flow trajectories. Therefore, passen-
gers often have multiple routes to choose while moving within the hub. These routes can be enumerated by using an effective
route-searching algorithm. Passengers make their route choices based on their perception of the instantaneous route travel time at
the current moment and information about the hub passenger flow network. This allows them to reach their destination platform
or exit quickly.
Since passengers are typically time-sensitive travelers with precise destinations, they will choose the route with minimal travel
time at the current moment as their optimal choice to reach their target platform or exit. However, passengers cannot have full
access to real-time information about the hub passenger flow network and actual flow distribution. Hence, there are errors in their
perception of the travel time function for routes. When each passenger chooses the route with the minimum perceptual travel time
at the current moment and cannot achieve a better strategy through unilateral changes, the network attains the state of Dynamic
Stochastic User Optimal (SDUO) equilibrium at that instant (Ran and Boyce, 2012). For practical computational purposes, this study
discretizes the investigated time interval: the time interval [0, 𝑇] is divided into 𝐾+ 1 periods, each denoted as 𝑘(0 ≤𝑘≤𝐾), and
the length of each period is 𝛥𝑡, such that 𝑇= |𝐾+ 1| 𝛥𝑡. The discretization principle ensures that passengers entering any link or
node within a certain period cannot leave that link or node within the same period.

The dynamic changes in passenger numbers on various links, as shown in Fig. 10, indicate that some links quickly return to

struggle to quickly return to their initial state after reaching peak passenger numbers. This is because they are restricted by the

5. Conclusions
This paper presents a spatial–temporal distribution model for passenger flow that considers queuing at crucial nodes in passenger
transit hubs. Passageways, stairs, and other passenger access facilities are represented as links, and essential areas, such as service
facilities and spatial connections, are represented as nodes. Thus, a passenger flow network is established that comprehensively
considers the hub’s complex spatial structure and passenger flow trajectories. Considering the queuing and congestion at crucial
facilities within the hub, the instantaneous travel time functions for links and nodes are defined in the network and a passenger
travel time model is constructed. A dynamic route choice model based on the Logit model is proposed to approach passengers’ choice
of routes in the hub. Additionally, a dynamic passenger flow loading model is developed. These components constitute the passenger
flow spatial–temporal distribution model for passenger transit hubs. This model is employed to calculate the real-time distribution
of passenger flows under varying passenger inflow rates. Based on the model’s characteristics, a solution algorithm is developed.

Additionally, two different passenger flow scenarios are designed in the numerical examples, and the results are compared with
those obtained from the AnyLogic simulation platform to further validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed model.
The passenger flow network proposed in this study is built based on a general understanding of the internal structure and
characteristics of hubs, demonstrating flexibility and universality. By adjusting the network structure, as well as the information
of links and nodes, it can be applied to various types of real-world hubs, including subway stations, railway stations, airports,
etc. The proposed travel time model can be calibrated and optimized by incorporating real-world data, enhancing the accuracy of
the computational results. Overall, this model can be adjusted and customized according to the specific conditions and passenger
demands of individual hubs. The model proposed in this paper is among the first to consider dynamic passenger loading and
dynamic route selection in hub scenarios. It has the capability to predict the dynamic distribution of passenger flows within hubs by
integrating real-time passenger flow data. Its unique advantages and application prospects make it a model of significant importance.
Through further research and practical implementation, the model proposed in this paper is expected to provide effective theoretical
support and decision-making references for optimizing the design and operation of transportation hubs.
This study can be improved in future studies. For instance, the passenger flow spatial–temporal distribution model established in
this paper is based on route choice, meaning that once passengers choose a route to their destination, they cannot change it. However,
passengers’ movement within the hub may not strictly adhere to this assumption. In future modeling, consider the current location
of passengers and take into account factors such as congestion levels and directional signage to make more dynamic decisions
about their next steps. Furthermore, this paper did not validate the model with real-world hub cases and data. In future research,
representative real hub cases will be selected for in-depth study. The model will be calibrated and optimized through field surveys
and data collection to enhance its accuracy and applicability. Subsequently, future research will focus on applying the optimized
model to more real-world cases and promoting the research outcomes in practical transportation management and planning to
enhance the operational efficiency and passenger experience of hubs. Additionally, exploration will be conducted into utilizing the
model for emergency situation prediction and decision support to improve the hubs’ responsiveness and safety.
